title: In vitro simulation of drinking events in cattle☆☆☆
author: Rahman, Chlingaryan, et al.

steps.title: Gather equipment and materials
steps.instruction: Collect all items listed for the simulation: food‑grade stainless steel water bath (20 L), heating immersion circulator, temperature data logger and reader, cold water (≤4 °C), plastic bucket, plastic tray, over‑sink rack, plastic mug or beaker, and a 250 mL fermentation jar.

steps.title: Prepare water bath
steps.instruction: Fill the 20 L stainless steel water bath with water, place the heating immersion circulator in the bath and set it to maintain a temperature of approximately 39 °C (the normal reticulorumen temperature).

steps.title: Position fermentation jar
steps.instruction: Place the 250 mL fermentation jar inside the water bath, using the plastic bucket, tray, or over‑sink rack as needed to keep the jar stable and fully immersed.

steps.title: Create temperature drop
steps.instruction: Add cold water (≤4 °C) to the water bath to lower the bath temperature by about 9 °C. The jar temperature will reach its minimum after a lag of 6–7 minutes, then begin to recover.

steps.title: Record temperature data
steps.instruction: Connect the temperature data logger to both the water bath and the fermentation jar, start logging, and record temperature observations every 3 seconds for at least 120 minutes to capture the full recovery to the pre‑event temperature of 39 °C.

steps.title: Simulate multiple drinking events
steps.instruction: If additional drinking events are required, adjust the iteration number in the heating device software and repeat the cold‑water addition step for each event.

steps.title: Analyze temperature data
steps.instruction: Import the logged data into R, create a continuous bath‑temperature function using ‘approxfun’ with linear interpolation between 3‑second points, numerically integrate with the ‘integrate’ function, and estimate the cooling‑rate constant kj by least‑squares minimisation (kj ≈ 0.33). Compute the root‑mean‑square error (RMSE ≈ 0.22 °C) to assess model fit.
